purpose: This JSON serves as persistent project memory or handoff document. When starting a new conversation with any AI, provide this file to instantly convey the complete project context including architecture, file structure, known issues, and recommended improvements. The AI should use this as a roadmap to understand where code lives, what's broken, and what needs fixing - then ask for specific files or code snippets as needed.

project._meta: Core identity for this project - name, version (bump patch for fixes, minor for features, major for architecture changes, per ai_maintenance), a one-line human-readable description, and this file's own filename/relative path. Architecture and feature detail live in core_features and known_limitations, not here.
project.name: Pool Chemistry Assistant
project.description: Desktop app that analyzes pool water chemistry test results and gives dosing/SLAM-recovery guidance, for a home pool owner managing their own pool.

ai_instructions._meta: This section is instructions to the AI, functionally equivalent to a _meta field even though it's broken into multiple named fields (ai_usage, ai_maintenance, etc.) for readability -- the same rule applies: every field in this section, including this one, is set by the user and must NEVER be modified, rewritten, summarised, or removed by an AI, even during routine end-of-session updates elsewhere in the file. New ai_* fields may be added when the user explicitly asks for a new standing instruction. Existing ones are never touched without an explicit request to change that specific instruction -- not because a session judges the wording outdated, redundant, or removable.
ai_instructions.ai_usage: Use this context to understand project architecture before suggesting fixes. Reference the file_structure to know where functionality resides. Check known_limitations and incomplete_features before recommending solutions. Use recommended_improvements as a prioritized task list when the user asks for next steps. Ask for specific files from the structure below rather than assuming code locations. When updating this file after a session, keep only the 5 most recent entries in recent_fixes — remove the oldest entries to prevent bloat.
ai_instructions.ai_maintenance: At the end of each session, offer to update this file. Update project.version (increment patch for fixes, minor for new features, major for architecture changes) -- but only once per session unless the user explicitly starts a new, distinct piece of work; related follow-ups, confirmations, or closures that land later in the same sitting belong in that same version bump and the same recent_fixes entry, not a new one. Update project.description if the app's purpose or scope changes. Add a recent_fixes entry summarising what changed. Update any sections that were affected by the session's changes. Remove resolved known_limitations entries rather than marking them resolved in place — the resolution narrative belongs in recent_fixes, not as a longer-lived entry elsewhere. When providing updates, give only the targeted fields that changed — do not rewrite or reprint the entire file. This keeps updates fast and easy to apply manually. Present the changed fields in the same order they appear in the actual context.json being updated, top to bottom, rather than grouping by perceived importance or the order they came up in conversation — this makes the presented diff easier to apply by hand, since scrolling through it matches scrolling through the real file. Entirely new fields or sections that don't yet exist in the file have no position to match — present those last, after all updates to existing fields.
ai_instructions.ai_current_state_vs_history: The current-state sections (core_features, calculation_constants, target_ranges, slam_lifecycle, file_structure, key_classes, key_methods, key_rules, known_limitations, etc.) must describe ONLY what the system currently is and does -- the present configuration, the present behavior, the present reason it's built that way. They are NOT a logbook. The chronological story of what changed, when, and why -- dated edit history, superseded approaches, 'was X, now Y' transitions -- belongs exclusively in recent_fixes. When updating a current-state section, REPLACE the outdated description with the new current state rather than appending the change onto the end; the fact that it changed is captured by the corresponding recent_fixes entry, not by a trail left inside the section. The one deliberate exception is a not-yet-verified or provisional status ('applied but not yet confirmed working'), which IS current-state information a future session needs and belongs in known_limitations until resolved. If a current-state section has accumulated embedded history over past sessions, trimming it back to pure current-state during an unrelated update is encouraged, not a violation of the 'only touch what changed' rule. Not all current-state sections carry the same amount of detail, and that's intentional: file_structure and core_features are NAVIGATIONAL -- a map pointing at where to look, kept to the length caps in their own _meta, since the how lives in the code. key_rules, critical_config_notes, and known_limitations are the opposite -- they exist specifically to capture non-obvious facts that are genuinely expensive to rediscover, so precision and completeness there is the section doing its job, not bloat to trim.
ai_instructions.ai_prune_on_drift: At the start of a session, after reading this file, assess whether any current-state section has drifted into logbook style -- embedded dated entries, stacked 'UPDATED <date>:' or 'was X, now Y' fragments, multi-paragraph fields where most of the content is history rather than present state, or the same change narrated both in a section and in recent_fixes. If it has, proactively tell the user the file looks like it has accreted history in place. Always surface this and get explicit approval before pruning -- this applies even to an AI with direct file access to this repository; noticing drift is not itself permission to fix it, the same as ai_context_updates' direct-edit permission is not permission to prune unprompted or silently fold it into unrelated work. Once approved, prune it back to current-state (delegating the history to recent_fixes and cross-references) the same disciplined way a dedicated cleanup session would -- one section at a time. An AI with direct file access applies the pruned fields directly (context.json is git-tracked, so no separate backup is needed -- git history already covers that); an AI without file access instead presents each trimmed field for the user to review and apply by hand. This is a safeguard against exactly the drift that ai_current_state_vs_history exists to prevent -- the two work together: one keeps clean files clean, the other recovers files that were already dirtied before the rule existed.
ai_instructions.ai_context_updates: When updating context.json at session end: if the AI has direct read/write access to this repository's files (e.g. Claude Code or an equivalent agent with a file-edit tool), apply the changes directly to context.json with that tool rather than only printing them in chat -- still summarise what changed, labelled by key name, so the user can review it, but the file on disk should already reflect the update by the time the summary is given. If the AI does NOT have direct file access (a chat-only interface with no way to write to the user's machine), DO NOT rewrite the entire file -- present only the sections that changed or need to be added, clearly labelled by their key name, and let the user manually apply them. Either way: never rewrite the entire file when only a few fields changed, never touch '_meta' fields, and follow ai_maintenance's other rules (version bump discipline, current-state-vs-history separation, recent_fixes trimmed to 5, field order when presenting for manual apply).
ai_instructions.ai_git_workflow: When a session's code changes are committed, include the corresponding context.json update (version bump plus recent_fixes entry) in that same commit rather than as a separate follow-up, so the spec doc and the code it describes never drift apart in git history.
ai_instructions.ai_token_warning: Periodically assess whether the conversation is getting long (many file pastes, long back-and-forth, large code blocks). When it feels like the context window is getting full, proactively flag it to the user. If the AI has direct file access, apply any pending context.json updates immediately rather than waiting for session end -- the file is the persistent source of truth, so nothing is lost if the conversation is abandoned, compacted, or a fresh one is started, and the user doesn't need to manually copy/paste anything. If the AI does NOT have direct file access, remind the user to copy the latest context.json content to their local file and start a fresh conversation with it attached. Either way: do not wait until quality degrades — flag it early while there is still enough context to update the file cleanly.
ai_instructions.ai_model_recommendation: At the start of every session, after reading this context.json, recommend a Claude model and effort level before any work begins. Base the recommendation on: (1) project maturity and test coverage, (2) complexity of the work implied by recommended_improvements.immediate, (3) whether the session involves safety-critical logic, architectural changes, or routine feature/styling work. Format: one short paragraph stating the recommended model, effort level, and the reasoning. Do this before asking for any files or starting any task.
ai_instructions.ai_model_recheck: Mid-session, if the actual work turns out significantly more complex than recommended_improvements.immediate implied — for example, a bug traced back to an architectural issue, unexpected interactions between systems, or safety-critical logic discovered during implementation — pause and flag it. State the original recommendation, explain what changed, and suggest whether to upgrade model or effort level before continuing. Do not silently continue at the original settings if the complexity has materially increased.
ai_instructions.ai_conventions: Fields named '_meta' are structural instructions to the AI about how to interpret the section they belong to. They are NOT placeholders for project data and must NEVER be modified, summarised, or replaced. When filling in a new context.json from the template, copy every '_meta' value exactly as written -- word for word. When updating an existing context.json, leave every '_meta' value completely untouched. If you find yourself writing project-specific content into a '_meta' field, stop -- you are making an error.
ai_instructions.ai_python_whitespace: The user edits Python files by hand using tabs -- a deliberate habit, not an oversight -- but the files themselves have accumulated space-indentation over many sessions of AI-provided copy-paste snippets, so the established convention in any given .py file is very likely spaces even though his own typing habit is tabs. Two standing rules: (1) When providing a code snippet or diff for a .py file, check the file's EXISTING indentation first (view it, don't assume) and match that exactly, rather than defaulting to whatever formatting an AI would normally produce. (2) After ANY manual edit to ANY .py file -- typed by hand or pasted from an AI response -- run 'cat -A <file> | grep "\^I"' before trusting the file; empty output means clean, any printed line has a tab hiding in it.
ai_instructions.ai_secrets_handling: This app has no API keys or external service credentials -- its config files (pool_config.txt, dilution_config.txt) only ever hold pool volume, chemical percentages, and local file paths, and both are gitignored as personal runtime data rather than source. If a feature ever introduces a real secret, route it through a .env file or OS secrets store rather than hardcoding it, and never paste a live secret into chat.

core_features._meta: List each major feature as a single key-value pair. The key is a short feature name, the value is ONE TO THREE SENTENCES: what it does, where its entry point is, and (only if genuinely load-bearing) the runtime flag/state variable it depends on. Focus on the what and where — the how lives in the code. Drift signal: if an entry runs past 3 sentences, or contains a version tag ('v1.2.3', 'as of', 'now includes') or a fix narrative, that's implementation detail or history leaking in — trim it out per ai_current_state_vs_history; the removed detail isn't lost, it's already in the code and in git log/recent_fixes.
core_features.slam_detection: Automatically detects pre-SLAM, during-SLAM, post-SLAM, and post-SLAM final stages based on water clarity, chlorine levels, CYA, and overnight test results.
core_features.slam_timing: Time-of-day awareness for the initial shock: a pre-SLAM report generated more than ~2 hours before sunset carries a 'hold this dose until ~<cutoff>' banner on the SLAM_DOSES block and annotates SLAM PROCESS step 2, so the user doesn't start the shock in daytime UV. The cutoff tracks today's real, seasonal sunset, computed offline from the machine's location (sun_times, inferred from the Windows time zone) with no network call, no third-party dependency, and no user input; it falls back to a fixed afternoon hour when location/sunset can't be determined. Gates only the initial pre-SLAM push; active-SLAM top-ups are unaffected.
core_features.state_tracking: Remembers previous session states, detects suspicious transitions (algae→milky without overnight test), asks intelligent questions. Also flags a saved water clarity/SLAM state as potentially stale (e.g. pool drained/refilled) when last_seen_date shows a gap of 14+ days, and offers to reset to fresh defaults.
core_features.dilution_calculator: Standalone tool for testing high chlorine levels (>10 ppm). Configurable test kit range, auto-copies results to main field.
core_features.chemistry_calculations: pH, TA, chlorine, CYA, calcium hardness with proper dosing based on pool volume and chemical concentrations.
core_features.overnight_test: Tracks FC loss test status (not_tested/passed/failed) with automatic reset logic based on SLAM mode and water clarity.
core_features.history: Saves all calculations with timestamped entries to pool_history.txt
core_features.guidance_builder: Structured output formatting using GuidanceBuilder class for consistent, professional recommendations.

calculation_constants._meta: Reference dosing ratios that CALCULATION_CONSTANTS in pool_tool.py scales by pool volume and chemical concentration. Each value is the base dose for a 10,000L pool at the stated concentration.
calculation_constants.acid_ph_dose: 120 ml 31.45% HCl to drop pH 0.1 in 10,000L
calculation_constants.acid_ta_dose: 120 ml 31.45% HCl to drop TA 10 ppm in 10,000L
calculation_constants.baking_soda_ta_dose: 180 g to raise TA 10 ppm in 10,000L
calculation_constants.cal_hypo_dose: 15.38 g 65% cal-hypo to +1 ppm FC in 10,000L
calculation_constants.cya_dose: 10 g to raise CYA 1 ppm in 10,000L
calculation_constants.calcium_dose: 11 g CaCl2 to raise CH 1 ppm in 10,000L

target_ranges._meta: Ideal range (and target value where applicable) for each tested chemistry parameter. Mirrors TARGET_RANGES in pool_tool.py.

water_clarity._meta: Water clarity options offered in the UI dropdown and what a non-obvious state implies for SLAM staging.
water_clarity.milky_note: Typical after SLAM (dead algae) - focus on filtration, not chlorine

slam_lifecycle._meta: The SLAM lifecycle stages detect_slam_context() can return, and the water/chemistry condition that defines each one.
slam_lifecycle.pre_slam: Algae detected, chlorine below shock level
slam_lifecycle.during_slam: Chlorine at/above shock level, actively killing algae
slam_lifecycle.post_slam: Water milky, chlorine dropping toward maintenance
slam_lifecycle.post_slam_final: Overnight test passed, focusing on filtration

key_rules._meta: Non-obvious domain invariants that an AI must know before suggesting changes. These are rules that are correct by design but look wrong at first glance, or rules whose violation would cause subtle hard-to-debug behaviour. Do not duplicate things already in critical_config_notes (which covers configuration and build gotchas) or architecture_notes (which covers structural decisions). This section is for domain logic invariants — calculation rules, business rules, physical constraints, protocol rules. Remove this section if the project has no such rules.
key_rules.ph_reading_accuracy_during_slam: pH readings are INACCURATE when FC > 10 ppm (SLAM mode shows warning)
key_rules.overnight_test_auto_reset: Overnight test auto-resets: off when SLAM mode off, or when algae present, or clear water normal mode
key_rules.post_slam_final_trigger: Milky water + passed overnight test = post-SLAM final stage (focus on filtration)
key_rules.cya_dosing_timing: CYA dosing: complete SLAM FIRST, THEN add CYA (adding mid-SLAM raises shock level)
key_rules.acid_dose_splitting: Large acid doses: auto-split into multiple doses based on pool volume (1.5% threshold)
key_rules.chlorine_dose_splitting: Large chlorine raises: auto-split into multiple doses during maintenance (SLAM allows single dose)
key_rules.acid_chlorine_gas_risk: HCl and chlorine products release toxic chlorine gas if combined -- when a report includes both an acid (HCl) dose and any chlorine-raise dose, adjust_pool() attaches a safety warning telling the user to dose them separately (pump running, different spots), waiting for the first to circulate before adding the next. The wait time reuses get_waiting_time(V, pump, 'acid') -- the same turnover-based figure shown elsewhere in the report -- rather than a fixed number, and the mobile app (MobilePoolTool) uses the equivalent turnover calculation for consistency. Detection must cover both forms the doses take: an acid dose is any pH/TA entry that LOWERS pH or TA (matched via the _is_acid_dose helper on 'hcl'/'acid'/'ph high' in the action text, since pH-reduction strings name no chemical and only TA-reduction strings contain the literal 'HCl' token), and a chlorine dose includes the pre-/during-SLAM shock dose that lives in the SLAM_DOSES block (tracked by has_slam_chlorine_dose) as well as regular maintenance chlorine doses in regular_doses. Never present combined/simultaneous HCl+chlorine dosing instructions.
key_rules.slam_pump_continuous: During pre-/during-SLAM the PUMP GUIDANCE section advises running the pump continuously (24/7) via _slam_pump_guidance(), matching SLAM PROCESS step 5 and TFP practice (max circulation spreads chlorine and filters dead algae). This deliberately overrides the energy-saving maintenance runtime (turnover*2-4) used in normal mode -- don't 'optimize' SLAM pump runtime back down. post_slam/post_slam_final keep their own higher filtration runtime (recovery, not shocking).
key_rules.slam_report_dedup: In pre-SLAM/during-SLAM reports each section owns one job; generic instruction lists are suppressed so the SLAM protocol isn't repeated. The MAINTENANCE TIPS block is emitted only for normal/post_slam/post_slam_final (not pre/during -- the SLAM PROCESS checklist and SLAM MAINTENANCE section already cover test/brush/pump/filter); the WATER CLARITY block is skipped for green/black algae during a SLAM (its guidance duplicates the protocol and its status repeats the Parameters line); and calculate_chlorine_addition_options no longer appends a brush/pump note to the SLAM_DOSES block. Don't re-add these as a 'more guidance is better' pass -- the duplication (brush x4, pump 24/7 x3, etc.) actively confused a real read.
key_rules.slam_dose_render_order: GuidanceBuilder.SECTION_ORDER renders DOSEAGES (the CHEMICAL DOSES block, which carries the pH/acid dose and the pre-SLAM 'SLAM PROCESS' checklist) BEFORE SLAM_DOSES (the chlorine shock dose) on purpose, so the report reads top-to-bottom as 'correct pH first, then chlorinate' -- matching TFP SLAM and the checklist's own step 1. Do not reorder SLAM_DOSES back above DOSEAGES as a tidy-up; that reintroduces the contradiction where the chlorine dose appears above the pH step.
key_rules.slam_shock_timing: The initial SLAM chlorine shock should not be started in daytime UV -- chlorine added in the morning/midday is burned off before it kills much algae, worst at low/unknown CYA. _shock_timing() sets a cutoff SLAM_SHOCK_SUNSET_LEAD_HOURS (2) before today's real sunset; sunset comes from sun_times.local_sunset() (NOAA formula + representative coordinates for the machine's Windows time zone, read from the registry via winreg -- fully offline, no dependency, no user input). When sunset can't be determined (off Windows, zone absent from WINDOWS_TZ_COORDS, or polar day/night) it falls back to the fixed SLAM_SHOCK_EARLIEST_HOUR (16). adjust_pool()/get_slam_guidance_structured() take an injectable `now` (GUI passes nothing -> real local clock); local_sunset() also takes injectable coords/utc_offset_hours for testing. Pre-SLAM-only gate: surfaces a timing banner + step-2 annotation (naming today's sunset and the cutoff when known), never suppresses dose amounts, never applies to during-SLAM top-ups. Late evening/night is intentionally fine (past the cutoff, no UV).
key_rules.chlorine_dose_rounding: Cal-Hypo and liquid chlorine doses in calculate_chlorine_addition_options() round to the nearest whole g/ml, not the nearest 10 -- a deliberate choice made to match the mobile app's (MobilePoolTool) precision, not an oversight.

file_structure._meta: List every file that contains meaningful logic. This is a MAP, not a manual -- for each file, give one to two sentences: its role, and at most 1-3 entry-point classes/methods (only what a future session needs to know WHICH file to open for a given feature or bug -- never helper/private functions, never a full method inventory). If you want to know exactly what a function does, read the code. Drift signal: an entry longer than ~2 sentences, or containing a version tag ('v1.2.3', 'as of') or a fix narrative, means implementation detail or history has leaked in from a session's edit -- trim it back per ai_current_state_vs_history; nothing is lost, git log and recent_fixes already have it.
file_structure.pool_tool.py: Main application file. Contains PoolChemistryApp, DilutionCalculatorWindow, AppState, ToolTip classes.
file_structure.guidance_builder.py: GuidanceBuilder class for structured output formatting. Handles bullet points, sections, emojis, and clean formatting.
file_structure.sun_times.py: Offline sunset calculation for the SLAM shock-timing cutoff: WINDOWS_TZ_COORDS (Windows time zone -> representative city coords), get_local_coords() (reads the zone from the registry via winreg), the NOAA _sunset_utc_hours(), and local_sunset(). No network, no third-party dependency; returns None to trigger the caller's fixed-hour fallback when location/sunset is unavailable.
file_structure.pool_config.txt: Configuration file (auto-created): pool volume, chemical percentages, water clarity, overnight test status, previous state.
file_structure.pool_history.txt: History file with timestamped calculation results.
file_structure.dilution_config.txt: Configuration file (auto-created) for DilutionCalculatorWindow: test kit range, dilution ratio, auto-fill preference.

key_classes._meta: Each class with its core responsibility. Companion to file_structure — file_structure says where a class lives, this says what it does.
key_classes.PoolChemistryApp: Main application. Handles UI, config loading/saving, calculation orchestration, SLAM detection.
key_classes.DilutionCalculatorWindow: Standalone dilution calculator. Configurable test kit range, auto-saves settings, auto-fills chlorine field.
key_classes.AppState: Runtime state container. Stores config, window references, UI component references.
key_classes.GuidanceBuilder: Output formatter. Builds structured recommendations with proper sections and emojis.

key_methods._meta: The most important methods in the calculation pipeline (not every method) with a one-line description of its role.
key_methods.adjust_pool: Main analysis engine. Returns formatted recommendations using GuidanceBuilder.
key_methods.detect_slam_context: Determines SLAM lifecycle stage based on parameters.
key_methods.get_slam_guidance_structured: Returns structured SLAM guidance with doses, maintenance, protocols.
key_methods.calculate_safe_doses: Centralized safety calculator for chemical doses. Handles splitting, warnings.
key_methods._calculate_ph_alkalinity_combined_action: Combined pH/TA logic with centralized safety.
key_methods._calculate_ph_only_actions: Primary source for pH chemical doses.
key_methods.calculate_chlorine_addition_options: Returns structured chlorine dose data for builder.

data_flow._meta: Sequence of function calls for each major user-facing workflow. Companion to key_methods — this shows call order, key_methods describes what each does.
data_flow.calculation: User inputs test results → Calculate → adjust_pool() → detect_slam_context() → get_slam_guidance_structured() → chemistry calculations → GuidanceBuilder builds output → Scrollable results window → Save to history
data_flow.dilution: Open Dilution Calculator → Configure test kit (optional) → Select ratio → Recipe appears → Test diluted sample → Enter reading → Calculate actual FC → Auto-fills main chlorine field (if enabled)
data_flow.state_transitions: App loads config → detect_state_transition() compares previous vs current → Asks questions if suspicious → Updates config if user confirms

known_limitations._meta: Each entry describes a limitation, why it exists, and whether it is a hardware constraint, a known bug, or deferred work. Remove entries promptly once resolved — a stale limitation is worse than no entry at all.
known_limitations.ph_accuracy: pH readings flagged as inaccurate when FC > 10 ppm — chemical limitation, not an app bug.
known_limitations.dilution_assumes_distilled: Dilution calculator assumes distilled water for dilution. No adjustment for tap water mineral content.
known_limitations.history_growth: History file can grow large with no auto-pruning. Tracked under recommended_improvements.
known_limitations.cal_hypo_default: Cal-Hypo calculations assume 65% concentration if not specified by user.
known_limitations.sunset_location_granularity: SLAM shock-timing sunset is computed from the machine's Windows time-zone representative city, not the user's exact coordinates -- determining exact lat/long automatically offline isn't possible without user input or a network call, and Kevin chose the offline timezone approach. Accurate to ~10-15 min, fine for a 2-hour cutoff. Non-Windows systems and time zones absent from sun_times.WINDOWS_TZ_COORDS fall back to the fixed-hour cutoff (SLAM_SHOCK_EARLIEST_HOUR).
known_limitations.dosing_ignores_density: Volumetric (ml) acid/chlorine dosing scales by stated weight-percent only (e.g. 31.45/hcl, 12.5/bleach) and ignores solution density, so a user measuring diluted acid BY VOLUME is still under-dosed (~8% at 15%, ~11% at 10%; negligible at the standard ~31-32% Kevin uses) -- deferred, not a bug. The weight-mode feature (acid_weight_mode) already applies density for users who measure acid on a kitchen scale, via hcl_density()/fmt_acid(). Correct volume = base_ml * (31.45/c) * (rho_base/rho_c), rho ~ 1.16 at 31.45%, ~1.07 at 15%, ~1.05 at 10%. Fully resolving the volumetric case needs a density (or density-vs-% curve) per product applied in the ml math itself; implement only when a sub-20% product is actually measured by volume. Mirror of same entry in MobilePoolTool context.

recommended_improvements._meta: Priority flows top to bottom — both across sections (immediate before structural before planned before suggested) and within each section (first entry is highest priority). 'immediate' = highest priority work for the next session, whether a fix or a feature. 'structural' = refactors or architectural improvements that reduce future pain. 'planned' = committed features or milestones not yet started. 'suggested' = unvetted ideas from the session, not yet committed. Promote suggested → planned once decided, planned → immediate or structural once actively being worked. An optional 'next_priority_order' array may sit alongside these four buckets for a project complex enough that priority isn't simply immediate-then-structural-then-planned-then-suggested top to bottom -- list specific item keys (from any bucket) in the exact order they should be tackled. Omit it when category order alone is sufficient.

structural.history_pruning: Add auto-pruning to pool_history.txt to prevent unbounded growth.

dependencies._meta: External runtime requirements and the config files this app reads/writes at runtime. No external services — this app runs fully offline.

owner_pool_values_backup._meta: Recovery backup of the owner's stable pool-specific config values, kept here because pool_config.txt is gitignored personal runtime data with no automatic backup (see ai_secrets_handling) and was once silently wiped. Only the stable values belong here — NOT the transient session state (water_clarity, overnight_test, slam mode flags, last_seen_date, history_path), which is meant to change every run. If these ever go missing from pool_config.txt again, restore them from here. Keep in sync whenever the owner changes a pool value.

recent_fixes: Added an opt-in 'measure acid by weight' mode. Kevin doses acid off a kitchen scale whose 'ml' setting actually weighs grams (it assumes water's 1 ml = 1 g); HCl is ~1.16x denser, so weighing the raw ml figure under-dosed acid ~14% at 31.45%. New module-level hcl_density(pct) (linear rho = 1.0 + 0.005*pct, ~1% accurate 0-35%) and PoolChemistryApp.fmt_acid(ml), which renders every acid dose as grams (ml * density) when config.acid_weight_mode is on, else the unchanged 'X ml'. All internal dose/split math stays in ml (so the V*0.015 split thresholds are untouched) -- only the display converts. Routed all acid HCl output lines, the calculate_safe_doses acid split-instruction numbers, and get_high_dose_note through fmt_acid. Added a '⚖️ Measure acid by weight' checkbox to the config panel, persisted as acid_weight_mode in pool_config.txt (load_config default False; save_config writes it). Mirrored the whole feature in MobilePoolTool (Settings toggle + AppSettings/PoolConfig.acidWeightMode + fmtAcid across poolCalculations/chemicalCalculations/saltWaterCalculations). Verified 120 ml @31.45% -> 139 g, @15% -> 129 g, a headless Tk build, and mobile tsc --noEmit clean. The toggle persists immediately on change (on_acid_weight_mode_toggle writes acid_weight_mode to pool_config.txt, not only when Analyze runs), and every report's Parameters line now states Acid=weight (g) / volume (ml) via GuidanceBuilder.add_parameters, so the full report saved to history records which mode produced it.
